Approximately 2,145 trees expected to be felled

The current project is undertaken by a joint venture of "China State Construction Hong Kong", "Ameon", and "China State Construction Civil Engineering". According to a 2024 Legislative Council document, there are approximately 2,270 trees within the project scope, of which around 2,145 are expected to be felled, including 10 "trees of special value" – Aquilaria sinensis (Incense Tree) and 2 Ormosia pachycarpa. Authorities plan to replant approximately 2,140 trees upon completion, including Koelreuteria bipinnata (Golden Rain Tree), Magnolia grandiflora (Southern Magnolia), and Michelia champaca (Yellow Champaca), among others.

Loss of tree shade — residents: even more oppressive during hot weather

Our reporter recently inspected the area from Marina Cove to Sai Kung Town Centre and found that trees had been removed along sections at Pak Wai, Marina Cove, Pak Sha Wan, Pak Kong to Sai Kung Town Centre. Felling was particularly evident around Pak Kong. As land levelling works are underway, the reporter observed that nearly one-third of the trees on the hillside had been cut down; at least 15 consecutive trees had also been felled alongside the road near Tai Chung Hau Village. A village resident said that with the diminishing roadside greenery, the heat feels even more oppressive during hot weather.

Land levelling works are underway on the Pak Kong hillside, where trees have been felled.

The trunk of a felled large tree has been hollowed out with a hole, into which a bottle of orange juice has been placed.

Approximately 1,900 trees unavoidably need to be removed

The Highways Department, in response to The Collective's enquiry, stated that because the relevant works run very close to vegetation-covered slopes on both sides, some trees located mainly on the slopes need to be removed or transplanted to free up sufficient space for construction. After survey, it remains unavoidable that approximately 1,900 trees need to be removed.

13 Aquilaria trees — 11 expected to be felled

The authorities stated that there are 13 Aquilaria sinensis trees within the project scope. Of these, 11 were assessed as unsuitable for transplanting based on their form, structure, and growing location, and must be removed; the remaining 2 will be preserved in situ. In addition, one Ormosia pachycarpa was also assessed as unsuitable for transplanting and must be removed; one Camphor tree originally proposed for transplanting was likewise assessed to require removal after survey. Three Indian Banyan trees will be preserved in situ.

The authorities stated that the project team will plant approximately 2,000 trees at suitable locations within Sai Kung District, such as roadside greening belts, to enhance the roadside landscape and Sai Kung community environment.

Aquilaria classified as Vulnerable

Aquilaria sinensis is a native Hong Kong tree species, mainly distributed in Sai Kung, the northeastern New Territories, and around Lantau Island. As of 2021, there were approximately 5,000 mature Aquilaria trees in the territory. The species is classified as rare and is listed as a protected plant under the Protection of Endangered Species of Animals and Plants Ordinance, as well as being listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species. Because its resin can be refined into the precious fragrance "agarwood", in earlier years the territory — particularly around Sai Kung — saw mainland "tree-cutting gangs" coming to Hong Kong to fell them illegally, with black market prices exceeding tens of thousands of dollars.

As for Ormosia pachycarpa, it is a tree in the bean family (Fabaceae) genus Ormosia, classified by the Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department as a rare and precious plant. The species was first discovered in Happy Valley in 1850 and is now classified as Endangered within China.

Pak Wai Village resident Regina purchased a village house some years ago. Self-styled a "tree lover", her decision to buy was entirely due to an old tree in front of the house, which she likened to a "treasure". Upon learning of tree-felling in the surrounding area, she said emotionally: "It's 2,000 trees, not 200!" She believes Sai Kung has long been hailed as "Hong Kong's back garden" and questioned, "Without 2,000 trees, can Sai Kung still be called Hong Kong's back garden?"

Self-styled "tree lover" Regina decided to buy a house in Sai Kung entirely because of an old tree growing in front of it, which she described as finding a "treasure". (Provided by Regina)

She said that trees are alive and may take a century to grow; once lost, they cannot easily be restored — including the precious Aquilaria. Taking Pak Wai Village as an example, she noted that visitors may not remember the village name, but they remember an old tree at the village entrance, which has even become a bus stop landmark. "The reason I can see the mountain is because of these trees. Try removing the trees — how would I see the mountain?" She believes the government should not take a one-size-fits-all approach at the expense of nature conservation.

Residents deeply attached to old trees

Another Sai Kung resident, Amy, said that three generations of her family, including her children, have grown up in Sai Kung: "Seeing the trees gone — so many years of growing up are gone too." Without her glasses, she laughed that her eyesight has been excellent all these years precisely because of the surrounding greenery and the view of the forested hills. "Suddenly they cut them down, and the children will end up needing glasses."

Beyond witnessing the disappearance of trees, she lamented the changes she has seen in Sai Kung over the years — for example, several historic buildings facing the Sai Kung highway, including the 1946-established "China Paint" factory, known for its "Chrysanthemum", "Giraffe", and "Toy" brands, is to be demolished and redeveloped into housing. She also cited the recent case in which a typhoon brought down an old tree in the town, which attracted residents to "check in" — reflecting their deep emotional attachment to old trees.

Roadside has become "messy and unsightly"

Sai Kung resident Mr Tam said that although he does not know the exact number of trees felled, he has clearly seen the roadside trees diminish: "It used to be comfortable with so many trees, but now it just looks messy and uncomfortable." He noted that when he moved to Sai Kung one to two years ago, large-scale felling had not yet begun; he likewise felt it was a pity to see the Aquilaria cut down. He also questioned whether widening the road actually helps congestion, since traffic jams entering Sai Kung on holidays are expected anyway.

An 84-year-old Sai Kung resident known as "Uncle" has lived in the area for over 20 years. He said that after more than a thousand trees were felled, Sai Kung's landscape has become unrecognisable, and he questioned: "What do traffic jams have to do with those trees? Your cars don't drive through the trees, do they?"

Friends of the Earth director Wong Cheuk-yuet said that when project consultants assess trees, although it may not be intentional, for the convenience of construction it is easy to fall into a "nitpicking" situation — "if it can't be transplanted, just cut it down" — rather than making efforts to save each tree. For instance, ordinary species almost need to be "perfect" to be retained; even if a tree is in fair condition, as long as there are minor defects or slightly limited growing space, the report will list unfavourable factors. Some large trees may cost over a million dollars to transplant, or may decline due to procedures or difficulty in finding a suitable relocation site.

Aquilaria should in principle be preserved as far as possible

He acknowledged that some locations in Sai Kung are on slopes, where excavating soil and transplanting are more difficult, but if conservation is the goal, considerations should include heavy crown pruning, reducing the root ball size, and so on, with "preserving the species" and "saving its life" as the primary objective. With Aquilaria numbers having dropped sharply, they should in principle be preserved as far as possible. He also worried that as the road gains more traffic lanes and separation facilities, there will be insufficient space for planting along the route — turning what was once shaded by trees into large expanses of concrete, which in the long run may affect the experience of waiting for buses and walking.
